    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    According to recent reports, big gainers included W42ST, the Point/Plover Metro Wire, Grice Connect (“In the rural south, death is a large social driver”), and the Philomath News. Here’s our quarterly ranking of the top 25 local for-profit news sites in the United States.

    It’s time for our latest look at which newsrooms are having success increasing their web traffic. We bring you four of these each quarter, looking at four different market segments: local newspapers, nonprofit news outlets, public media stations, and for-profit local news sites. Rankings are based on estimates from Similarweb.

    Today’s edition looks at local for-profit news sites. (Eligible sites for this ranking are for-profit members of the trade group LION Publishers — LION standing for Local, Independent, Online News — so these are mostly digital-born newsrooms, not newspapers or TV stations.) The rankings for Q3 feature many of the same sites that performed well in our last edition. This time around, we’ve got details from local news sites in New York, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nevada, Georgia, and Oregon. Below that are the Top 25 rankings for July, August, and September.

    It has been revealed that W42ST In Newly introduced York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July. Publisher Phil O’Brien remarked that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST. “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.” O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s presently trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve debuted earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week. It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said. Point/Plover Metro Wire Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski. The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said. Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said. “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she said. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.” Grice Connect Statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July. DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position. But Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site. Philomath News The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath. Similarweb stats demonstrated a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he said. In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said. Oklahoma City Free Press, LINK nky, This Is Reno In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.” The Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews. Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.     Sources indicate that makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said.

    According to recent reports, “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she noted. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and newly introduced sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.”.

    Sources indicate that statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July.

    DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position.

    It has been revealed that but Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect rolled out free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site.

    The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath.

    Recent findings suggest that similarweb stats demonstrated a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he mentioned.

    In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he stated.

    In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.”.

    In a recent development, the Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews.

    Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.

    #227355. Industry News: B2B Podcasts Reach Buyers Search Can’t – Where Most Demonstrates Go Wrong

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1913 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: B2B Podcasts Reach Buyers Search Can’t – Where Most Demonstrates Go Wrong

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When HubSpot’s blog lost about 80% of its organic traffic to AI, revenue still grew nearly 20%.
    • It has been revealed that in his interview with Greg Jarboe for Search Engine Journal, CMO Kipp Bodnar explained why.
    • As a result, those newer channels now bring in about 90% of HubSpot’s content leads, with the blog accounting for roughly 10%.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When HubSpot’s blog lost about 80% of its organic traffic to AI, revenue still grew nearly 20%.

    It has been revealed that in his interview with Greg Jarboe for Search Engine Journal, CMO Kipp Bodnar explained why. In short, HubSpot had been building an audience outside search since 2021: a podcast network in 2021, a newsletter acquisition the same year, a creator program in 2022, and a YouTube network in 2023.

    As a result, those newer channels now bring in about 90% of HubSpot’s content leads, with the blog accounting for roughly 10%.

    It has been revealed that I’ve spent six years inside one of those channels. The agency I founded has produced more than 300 B2B podcasts since 2019 and booked more than 2,500 guest appearances for the companies behind them. (Disclosure: All first-hand figures in this article come from that work.) Reading the interview, what struck me wasn’t the traffic drop. Instead, it was that HubSpot’s recovery ran on the channel I know best, and that most of the patterns Bodnar described show up in our data every month, including the uncomfortable ones.

    In a recent development, so this article is about what a podcast does for a B2B company that a search result can’t. I’ve organized it around the four things a buyer has to do before they buy from you: notice you, hear you, trust you, and name you. It also covers where podcasts fail because a lot of them do!

    Industry observers note that bodnar’s most useful admission was that much of HubSpot’s lost traffic “was never going to turn into revenue.” For example, posts on famous quotes and emojis drew millions of visitors who would never buy software. When AI Overviews answered those questions directly, the visits disappeared, and very few of them were potential customers.

    Recent findings suggest that the mechanism is now well documented. Pages ranking first lose 58% of their clicks when an AI Overview appears, according to Ahrefs, up from 34.5% in its April 2025 run. Similarly, Pew Research found customers click a standard result 8% of the time when a summary appears, against 15% without.

    However, the crucial point is not that clicks fell. It is that search was always a weak way to build the thing B2B buyers actually use to decide: trust in a specific firm, earned from people they already believe.

    Reddit and SurveyMonkey’s 2026 research found 73% of B2B decision-makers trust peer recommendations, more than vendor websites at 55%. Meanwhile, Gartner found 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience. In other words, buyers want to learn from people like them, without being sold to. A 40-minute conversation between two practitioners is exactly that, in a form Google never ranked well, and AI engines are citing more and more.

    See also: The Dangerous Seduction Of Click-Chasing.

    According to recent reports, first, a podcast has to get a buyer to notice the firm behind it. This is where most B2B demonstrates fail, and I’ve watched this many times.

    A tech giant launches a show. The CEO hosts. Twelve episodes later, downloads are flat at 150 per episode, the CEO is bored, and the show quietly stops. The conclusion drawn is “podcasts don’t work for us.” In reality, the problem is that the show rolled out into nothing.

    Sources indicate that across the reveals we’ve produced, the ones that grow are the ones that start with an audience to grow from. Specifically, two things happen before episode one. The host appears as a guest on other shows the target buyers already listen to, so the first listeners arrive from a voice they trust. And the guest list is built from people with their own audiences, who then share the episode they’re in.

    HubSpot did a version of this at scale. The creator program and the podcast network were built years before the search traffic fell, so there was an audience waiting. Bodnar’s line that “no AEO trick would have covered an 80% hole” is therefore the same lesson at a different size.

    See also: The Latest Organic Growth Stack: Search, Social, Communities & AI.

    The second job is getting the buyer to listen.

    Instantly’s 2026 benchmark puts the average cold email reply rate at 3.43% across its platform, with the top 10% of senders getting past 10%. Instantly sells outbound software, so it has no reason to make those numbers look worse than they are.

    A podcast appearance inverts the dynamic. The buyer pressed play and they chose to spend 20 or 40 minutes with your leader, often while doing something else. A host they already trust vouched for your leader in the first 30 seconds.

    Sources indicate that when we track what happens after client appearances, the pattern is consistent. Inquiries arrive weeks later and quote the episode. In other words, the buyer heard the whole argument before they ever spoke to sales.

    For example, we regularly see leads come inbound to our clients saying: “I loved the episode on X with Y, I’d love to chat about Y for our business.”.

    The same applies to a company’s own show once it has listeners. Edison Research’s Infinite Dial 2026 puts monthly podcast listening at 58% of Americans aged 12 and over. The audience exists, but the question is whether your show gives them a reason to be in it, which brings us to the guests.

    The most reliable finding across our shows is also the one most companies resist. The fastest way into a buyer’s world is to interview them. Not a thought leader, not a partner, not a customer success story. The person you want to sell to.

    Recent findings suggest that one client, a risk-management software manufacturer, launched a weekly show in September 2025 hosted by its CEO, with guests drawn from the safety and risk leaders at its target accounts. (Disclosure: The company is a client of my agency, and these figures are from its public case study.) Twelve months later, roughly 20% of guests have become paying customers. The company also reported a 3.5x return on closed deals in the first six months, with more in the pipeline. Listeners who were never guests have become customers too, citing specific episodes as the reason they reached out.

    What made it work wasn’t production quality. Rather, it was three operational choices: a CEO who turned up every week, a conversation format that sets up a follow-up without being a pitch, and a post-recording workflow that got the sales team involved within days of each interview.

    In a recent development, remove any of the three and the show becomes content. With all three, it is a pipeline channel that happens to publish audio.

    This is also the part of podcasting that search can’t replicate, and never could. A buyer who spends an hour as a guest on your show has a relationship with your organization. By contrast, a buyer who clicked your blog post has a session.

    See also: How To Run A Webinar Program That Actually Drives ROI.

    The fourth outcome is the one Search Engine Journal readers will care about most, because it is where podcasts and AI search meet.

    Recent findings suggest that bodnar made two points about how HubSpot gets cited in AI answers. First, the engines lean on sources that aren’t your site: Reddit, LinkedIn, YouTube, and review sites. Second, prompts now run 40 to 100 words, so content has to “answer the full question in plain, chunked language, the way a buyer would ask it.” Consequently, HubSpot moved from “The Ultimate Guide to Content Marketing” to hyper-specific pieces built around real buyer situations.

    A podcast produces both of those things as a by-product. Every guest appearance is a mention, a link in show notes, and a transcript on someone else’s domain, which is the third-party presence engines weigh. Likewise, every episode of your own show is a transcript of a real buyer describing a real problem in their own words. That is the specific, first-party material engines can’t find anywhere else.

    We tested this on our own site. From June 1, 2026, we published one page a day written from our episode transcripts and case studies. Over the following months, our daily AI citations, which had sat between roughly 40 and 80 a day since the previous November, climbed to between 250 and 350 a day by October, and the number of our pages being cited rose from about 15 to around 60:.

    Daily AI citations and cited pages for the author’s website, November 2025 to October 2026. Image created by the author.

    It has been revealed that that said, I’d be cautious about the size of that effect. The base was small, and Bodnar is right that attribution here is correlative. But the direction matched what HubSpot saw: AI-answer visitors converting at roughly three times the rate of traditional search, because the buyer has already had the conversation.

    The practical implication for anyone running SEO is a show’s transcripts are a content source your competitors cannot copy, and the guest appearances are citations you don’t have to pitch for. Yet most companies with podcasts are sitting on both and using neither.

    The wins above come with a long tail of highlights that didn’t make it. Three failures account for most of them.

    The show introduces before anyone has borrowed an audience or booked the host on other shows. Twelve episodes, then silence. This is the majority of B2B podcast failures.

    Downloads are the podcast equivalent of the sessions Bodnar states HubSpot watched for 15 years. They are inflated by bots and repeat fetches, and they say nothing about who listened.

    It has been revealed that instead, the numbers that matter are which companies are listening, which guests became opportunities, and whether prospects mention the show when they inquire. If your hosting can’t tell you the first of those, you are flying blind.

    Recent findings suggest that the interview ends, the episode publishes, and then the guest never hears from the company again. The 20% conversion rate above came from a workflow, not a microphone.

    Greg Jarboe ended his write-up of the interview by arguing that the goal has changed. Inbound marketing was about showing up when a buyer searched. Now the buyer asks an AI first, and your manufacturer has to be the one they pick afterward. I agree, and I’d add that search alone can’t solve that problem.

    Industry observers note that buyers choose companies they have noticed, heard, trusted, and seen named. The places those four things happen are feeds, shows, and AI answers, not result pages.

    Industry observers note that A podcast is the one channel that can do all four at once. It borrows an audience through guesting, earns listening time no outbound sequence can, builds relationships with the buyers you interview, and produces the specific, first-party content AI engines cite. However, it is also slow, operationally demanding, and easy to do badly, which is why most of them stop at episode 12.

    Recent findings suggest that hubSpot built these channels with a large marketing team and a head start of several years. Most B2B companies have neither. That is an argument for starting now, not for not starting.

    Industry observers note that so before you count downloads, count buyers. How many of the people you want to sell to have been on your show, or listened to it?

    Confident kids, cautious elders: What we get wrong (and right) about who really understands social media algorithms

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    • Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address.

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    The generational edge that demonstrates up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

    Ask a 19-year-old how TikTok decides what to show them, and you’ll likely get a fast, confident answer about watch time, likes, and how “the algorithm just gets me.” Ask their grandmother, and you’re more likely to get a shrug.

    It has been revealed that the scene fits a story we’ve been telling for years: Young people are “digital natives” who intuitively grasp the platforms they grew up on, while older adults are outsiders, left behind and vulnerable. That story matters more than it used to. Algorithmically curated platforms are now a major source of news for Americans of all ages, which means people’s sense of how those systems work shapes how they judge the information they get there.

    But when you test what each group actually knows, rather than what they say they know, the story doesn’t hold up.

    RELATED ARTICLETrapped by what they know: Young adults’ algorithmic cynicismMyojung ChungNovember 17, 2025In a piece last year for Nieman Lab, I reported that young adults who spent more time on social media tended to know less about how algorithms work, and I speculated that constant use might create an illusion of understanding. My recent study published in Upcoming Media & Society set out to test that idea directly — measuring not just what people know, but how confident they are about it — across the full adult age range.

    Surveying 1,205 U.S. adults ages 18 to 65 and older, I measured two things. First, I asked people to rate their own understanding of how algorithms select, rank, and personalize content. Second, I measured their actual awareness of how these systems work, which covers content filtering, automated decision-making, data use, and algorithmic bias.

    Sources indicate that the self-ratings matched the conventional wisdom: Younger respondents rated their understanding significantly higher than older respondents did. But the awareness scores did not. Across every age group, actual awareness of how algorithms function was essentially flat.

    In other words, the generational edge that indicates up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

    Industry observers note that to capture this, I use the concept “algorithmic knowledge confidence”: the gap between what people believe they know and what they can demonstrate. When self-assessment outpaces actual awareness, that’s overconfidence; when it lags behind, that’s underconfidence. Young adults tended toward the former: They don’t necessarily understand algorithms better, but they feel more certain that they do. Older adults tended toward the latter: They don’t know less, but they’re more cautious about claiming what they know.

    According to recent reports, then why would the most-online generation feel the surest? Psychologists have long documented that people mistake familiarity for understanding. When something feels easy to process — often simply because we’ve encountered it many times — we tend to assume we understand it. This is called processing fluency.

    Industry observers note that exposure to social media differs sharply by age. About 95% of 18- to 29-year-olds use YouTube and about 63% use TikTok, according to Pew Research; among adults 65 and older, those figures drop to 64% and 12%. For younger users, algorithmic feeds are part of the daily routine, and that routine produces a comfortable sense of “I know how this works,” whether or not it’s true. Older adults, with less exposure, don’t get the same fluency cues, and default to more conservative self-assessments.

    Industry observers note that my data are consistent with this explanation. The number of platforms people used daily accounted for a meaningful share of the link between age and overconfidence: The more platforms someone used, the further their self-rated understanding outran their demonstrated awareness. Because this is a survey taken at one point in time, it can’t prove that heavy use causes overconfidence, but the pattern fits the fluency account well.

    According to recent reports, this miscalibration isn’t just a matter of bruised egos or modest grandparents. It shows up in how people evaluate the news and information in their feeds.

    RELATED ARTICLEWant to fight misinformation? Teach people how algorithms workMyojung ChungSeptember 4, 2024Younger adults who overestimated their algorithmic understanding were more likely to see the content in their feeds as reliable and trustworthy, and more likely to believe they were being exposed to a diverse range of viewpoints. Older adults who underestimated their understanding showed the opposite pattern: more skepticism about the reliability of what they saw, and a sense that their feeds were narrower than they might actually be.

    Recent findings suggest that other research points in the same direction for younger audiences. A Stanford study found that two-thirds of U.S. high school students couldn’t tell a news article from sponsored content, a reminder that growing up inside algorithmic feeds is no guarantee of being able to evaluate them.

    It has been revealed that but the older adults’ pattern isn’t a healthy one either. Blanket distrust is as poor a guide to information as blanket confidence. It can lead people to dismiss accurate reporting along with misinformation, or to disengage from platforms entirely rather than learning to use them critically.

    First, algorithmic literacy needs to teach calibration, not just content. Most digital literacy efforts focus on pouring in more information about how algorithms work. My findings suggest that’s only half the job. The other half is helping people accurately judge what they don’t know.

    Second, interventions should look different for different audiences. For younger, overconfident owners, that might mean exercises designed to puncture false certainty: quick self-assessments that reveal the gap between what someone assumes and what they can actually explain, or interactive demonstrations of common misconceptions about how feeds are built. For older, underconfident users, the goal isn’t to manufacture confidence. It’s to help them recognize the caution they already bring to online information as a genuine strength, and to pair it with the skills to tell trustworthy sources from untrustworthy ones, so that skepticism becomes discernment rather than disengagement.

    In a recent development, third, anyone trying to reach audiences through algorithmic platforms, from educators to newsrooms to the platforms themselves, should stop assuming that the youngest users are the savviest. Confidence and competence are different things, and treating one as a proxy for the other leaves both groups poorly served.

    The next time a young adult confidently explains “how the algorithm works,” it might be worth asking: How can you be sure you actually know that? And the next time an older relative shrugs and says they don’t think they get it, it might be just another kind of miscalibration — with costs of its own, just a quieter one.

    Myojung Chung is an associate professor of journalism and media innovation at Northeastern University and a faculty associate at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society at Harvard University.

    One of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The new bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, and MarketWatch.

    Industry observers note that as part of the shift, the manufacturer revised each site’s robots.txt file — a webpage that tells bots which parts of a site they can and can’t access. Rather than reactively blacklisting bots through robots.txt, Dow Jones now operates with a whitelist for select crawlers and scrapers.

    “As bot traffic has shifted from discovery-oriented use cases toward systems that can ingest, summarize, or otherwise benefit from our content without a relationship in place, we have moved to a more deliberate signal,” noted Nolly Evans, chief development officer at Dow Jones. “[This] signals to third parties that they must negotiate and partner directly with us for content access.”.

    The Wall Street Journal’s whitelist contains more than 60 bots, including search engine crawlers and three scrapers operated by OpenAI, which has a $250 million-plus licensing deal with Dow Jones’ parent organization, News Corp.

    “We’re seeing astronomical growth in bot traffic while human referrals and traffic to news sites are being curtailed,” mentioned Evans. “That’s a clear signal to publishers that the old norms are no longer working, and that something needs to change.”.

    In a recent development, robots.txt files are voluntary guidance for all bots, including those deployed by AI companies. They’re not hard technical blocks or legally binding contracts. Some AI companies, like Perplexity, have used “stealth crawlers” to bypass robots.txt files while evading detection. Still, The Journal isn’t alone in using robots.txt to disallow bots by default, whether to create friction for scrapers, as leverage to negotiate for content licensing deals, or to minimize the burden on their servers.

    An analysis of the robots.txt files of 1,000 leading English-language publishers websites by the bot analytics company Known Agents highlights that about 2% of those sites now disallow all bots by default, including Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Publishers Weekly, and the British technology news site The Register.

    Industry observers note that many of these publications are owned by News Corp, including several of the organization’s Australian newspapers (The Australian, The Daily Telegraph in Sydney, the Herald Sun in Melbourne) and its marquee U.K. papers (The Times, The Sun, The Scottish Sun).

    Sources indicate that “One of the most important issues for us is making sure that the IP journalists create is respected by the AI companies,” News Corp CEO Robert Thomson said in an interview with CNBC last week. “The principled companies want to have an agreement, and the unprincipled companies don’t. We’ll try to convince you to be transactional and pay us for our IP and pay us for our journalism, or we’ll sue you.”.

    More and more publishers are opting to restrict bots using whitelists. Late last year, The Atlantic told Digiday that it only allows bots associated with its licensing deals or those that drive significant traffic to the website. In June, Digiday first reported that Reuters and Time had started issuing whitelists of their own.

    It has been revealed that people Inc. has been vocal about its decision to go beyond robots.txt files and hard-block bots by default. When the company made the switch at the beginning of this year, it went from blocking 2,000 unique bots to more than 30,000.

    Many of these publishers are responding to a upcoming reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers. Over the past 90 days, around 34% of pageviews across more than 5,000 randomly selected websites came from bots, according to an index maintained by Known Agents. About 29% of those bots were “AI-related” (e.g. AI agents, AI chatbots, and AI training scrapers), as opposed to more traditional bots like search engine crawlers and archivers operated by the Wayback Machine.

    Recent findings suggest that despite some publishers wanting to restrict AI-related bot traffic, many aren’t making full use of their robots.txt files to do so, according to Gavin King, the CEO of Known Agents. The manufacturer started as a free crowdsourced database to help identify bots, but now offers publishers analytic tools and other products to monitor and control bot traffic.

    Known Agents at the moment tracks more than 2,000 AI-related bots, but the majority of English-language news publishers only restrict a fraction of those on their robots.txt files.

    According to recent reports, “Robots.txt is the easiest first line of defense,” mentioned King. “The fact that people are reaching out to [internet infrastructure companies to sign] six-figure year contracts instead of updating their robots.txt for free is such a miss.”.

    In a recent development, king acknowledged that robots.txt alone can’t stop content from being scraped without permission or compensation. But he also pointed to clients who have reduced traffic from known AI-related bots by more than 90% by updating their robots.txt file with a more comprehensive list.

    “It’s been such a manual process,” remarked King. “Everyone is doing it individually, in-house instead of automating the process.”.

    It has been revealed that slate is one of the publications that has leaned on Known Agents’ “Automated Robots.txt” to try to stem the tide of AI bots to its site. Slate’s small product team uses the free version of the tool to access Known Agents’ API weekly and review any newly discovered bots or renamed agents that have been added to the tech giant’s database. The tool automatically revises its robots.txt file based on that review.

    According to recent reports, “We have almost 30 years of content, which is a long history of being online,” Greg Lavallee, Slate’s VP of technology, stated. “We’re seeing no value from bots and it costs us bandwidth fees, so we decided to tell them not to bother.”.

    Industry observers note that lavallee noted that since September, preliminary data shows that several bots have ignored the publication’s robots.txt and continue to attempt to crawl its website, though he declined to name the exact bots. Slate is exploring “server-side paywall strategies that will make it more difficult for scrapers to access full content,” he said.

    Slate right now has no licensing deals with major AI companies, despite active outreach to buyers in the past.

    “It’s very easy for us to take that robots.txt list and go look at the [server] logs and say, ‘We told you not to access and then you did,” said Lavallee. “I feel like you have to [update your Robots.txt file], but it’s definitely not enough. Something more needs to happen than asking nicely.”.

    #227346. Paid Search Has An AI Blind Spot – IAB Blueprint Notes A Claim Is Not Credit via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1811 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Paid Search Has An AI Blind Spot – IAB Blueprint Notes A Claim Is Not Credit via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that if your branded search campaigns have posted their best return on ad spend of the year, the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) has a question you should answer before you ask for more budget.
    • 12, the IAB released its AI-Era Attribution Blueprint, a framework for sorting out what role AI played when someone buys something.
    • ChatGPT answer can create the intent, a branded query can capture it, and your Google Ads account can book the conversion as a brand campaign win.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that if your branded search campaigns have posted their best return on ad spend of the year, the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) has a question you should answer before you ask for more budget. Who, or what, created that demand in the first place?

    Sources indicate that on Nov. 12, the IAB released its AI-Era Attribution Blueprint, a framework for sorting out what role AI played when someone buys something. The report cites Similarweb data showing that consumers who got a brand recommendation from an AI assistant were 2.5 times more likely to visit that brand’s website within seven days. Only 8.8% of those visits came directly from AI referrals. Search was credited with 55.9% of them, and direct traffic with 19.9%.

    ChatGPT answer can create the intent, a branded query can capture it, and your Google Ads account can book the conversion as a brand campaign win.

    According to recent reports, the blueprint won’t tell you how much of your brand revenue fits that description. What it does give you is a standard of evidence for finding out, plus a few habits worth adopting in your accounts before the 2027 planning cycle locks in.

    The framework asks three questions of each conversion. Who or what created the intent? Who or what made the decision? Who or what completed the purchase?

    Sources indicate that the answers put the conversion in one of three pathways, labeled Human-Owned, AI-Assisted, and AI-Executed. According to AdExchanger’s account of the document:.

    The pathway then decides which parties are eligible to make a “decision claim” or a “contributory claim,” and what evidence each claim needs. The IAB’s release states, “A claim is not credit; it is the right to be evaluated for credit.”.

    Caroline Giegerich, the IAB’s VP of AI, framed the problem in terms every search marketer will recognize.

    “AI-influenced sales are sometimes reported as search or direct traffic, which can send the next marketing investment to the wrong channel,” she stated in the announcement. She added that the blueprint is meant to work alongside existing attribution systems, defining the extra credit claims AI creates and the evidence each one requires.

    In other words, nobody is asking you to rip out data-driven attribution. The blueprint sits on top of it.

    Sources indicate that the document also changed shape while it was being written. Giegerich told Digiday she went in expecting the working group to work out how credit gets assigned, and the document became “more of a call to action to the industry” instead. Digiday reported the effort took about four months and named working group members including People Inc., Walmart, WPP Media, Emberos, Criteo, Bluefish, Microsoft, Brandlight, Tinuiti, and Prudential Financial.

    Google is not among the members Digiday named, which matters for anyone hoping the largest search ad platform will start labeling AI-originated activity the way the blueprint asks.

    See also: AI Visibility Measurement: What To Track & What To Ignore.

    The IAB grounded the release in its own buyer research. In the 2026 Outlook Study: September Revision, 45% of ad buyers named comparing AI-driven and traditional customer journeys as their top measurement challenge, and 44% remarked they rely on branded search and direct traffic as proxies for AI influence they can’t track.

    It has been revealed that google’s own numbers show why this is getting harder to ignore. Alphabet reported Q3 2026 Google Search & other revenue of $63.35 billion, up 12% year-over-year, while CEO Sundar Pichai said Search query growth was the fastest it has been in five years. On the earnings call, chief business officer Philipp Schindler pointed to lower monetization of fast-growing AI Mode queries as one factor in the slower revenue growth, alongside currency effects, which he called the largest factor. More queries are flowing through AI surfaces, and the trail from those surfaces to the conversion is thinner than the trail from a classic results page.

    Here is my perspective. The most useful line in the blueprint for PPC managers, is that a claim is not credit. Platform attribution has blurred those two ideas for as long as I’ve covered this business, since 2003. Google Ads data-driven attribution spreads credit across the Google touchpoints it can observe. It cannot observe the ChatGPT conversation that sent someone to type your brand name. So, the report you trust most has a blind spot exactly where the newly introduced demand is being created.

    See also: When Attribution Looks More Precise Than The Data Behind It.

    Before anyone builds a budget case on 55.9%, it helps to know where that figure comes from.

    It originates in Similarweb’s June 2026 study, “The Downstream Impact of AI Visibility.” It used Similarweb’s U.S. desktop panel from July through December 2025, looked at ChatGPT recommendations, and studied three verticals through brand pairs (American Express and Capital One, Skyscanner and Kayak, Sephora and Ulta). Customers who named the brand in their own prompt were excluded.

    In a recent development, search accounted for 55.9% of AI-influenced visits versus 40.4% of visits that weren’t AI-influenced, a gap of 15.5 points. Direct traffic went the other way, 19.9% versus 38.8%. AI-influenced visitors also viewed about 12 pages per visit, compared with 6.5 for everyone else.

    It has been revealed that there are limits a practitioner should keep in view. The panel is desktop only, while a large share of shopping happens on phones. It covers ChatGPT, not Claude, Copilot, Gemini, or Google’s own AI Mode. Six brands is a small sample, and the published figures I could find report “search” as a channel without splitting paid clicks from organic ones, so nobody should claim from this study that a specific share went to Google Ads.

    According to recent reports, one more caution about the IAB survey. MediaPost reported that 44% of buyers named adapting to changing consumer behavior, including AI-driven search, as their top investment challenge. The release for the blueprint cites 44% relying on branded search and direct traffic as proxies. Same study, same percentage, different questions.

    Sources indicate that google Analytics added an “AI Assistant” channel to GA4’s Default Channel Group in May 2026, which sorts sessions from recognized chatbot referrers into their own row. It’s a real improvement, but it works on referrers. The shopper who reads a ChatGPT answer, opens a upcoming tab, and searches your brand indicates up as Paid Search or Organic Search, never as AI Assistant. That is the exact behavior the Similarweb data describes.

    See also: 81.8% Of My ‘AI Assistant’ Traffic Was Fake. The Googlebot Number Was Worse.

    Recent findings suggest that in the first edition of YouTube and Video Marketing, published in 2009, I quoted Galileo on page 337. “Count what is countable, measure what is measurable. What is not measurable, make measurable.” I’ve repeated it to students and clients ever since, because I haven’t found a better summary of what a marketer’s job is.

    The IAB blueprint reads like a working version of it for paid search.

    Count what is countable. Clicks, conversions, and sessions with an AI referrer are all countable, and your accounts already count them well.

    According to recent reports, measure what is measurable. Whether your brand campaigns create sales or simply catch them on the way to checkout can be measured with lift tests and holdouts. Most advertisers just haven’t done it.

    Then comes the hard part: What is not measurable, make measurable. Nobody outside the AI platforms can observe the ChatGPT conversation that sent a shopper to type your brand name into Google. The blueprint’s answer is to classify that conversion anyway, attach a claim to it, and spell out the evidence the claim would need. That is how something unmeasurable starts becoming measurable. It also tells you exactly what to ask for when the AI platforms are ready to share.

    It has been revealed that none of this requires the AI platforms to cooperate first. Here are four steps you can take now.

    1. Estimate your pathway mix. The blueprint’s first ask of brands is to estimate the share of their conversions in each pathway. The cheapest way to start is to ask customers. Add AI assistant options (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Copilot, Claude) to your post-purchase survey or lead form’s “how did you hear about us” question. Store the answer in your CRM. If you already import offline conversions, you can bring a self-reported “AI-assisted” signal into Google Ads as a separate conversion action set to secondary, so you can see it by campaign without letting it steer Smart Bidding.

    Industry observers note that 2. Put brand campaigns through an incrementality test. Google Ads help documentation now lists Search and Performance Max as supported campaign types for user-based Conversion Lift, with thresholds of at least 1,000 observed conversions and a minimum study campaign budget of $5,000. The same page still notes that Conversion Lift isn’t available for every account, so check with your rep. If you don’t qualify, a geo-based holdout on brand terms will tell you something useful. A lift test won’t classify the AI pathway for you. It will tell you how much of what your brand campaign claims would have happened anyway, which is the question you need answered before brand spend absorbs more of the budget.

    Industry observers note that 3. Report two columns, not one. The blueprint asks agencies to apply a single claim-and-evidence standard across platforms and to separate platform-reported claims from independently verified ones. Do that in your next Quarterly Business Review (QBR). Show Google Ads-reported brand conversions next to lift-tested incremental conversions, and show GA4’s AI Assistant sessions next to your survey’s self-reported AI share. When the columns disagree, that disagreement is the finding.

    It has been revealed that 4. Ask your platform reps how AI traffic is labeled. The blueprint asks AI platforms to disclose whether recommendations are paid or organic, to name the sources behind them, and to label AI-originated traffic consistently. Put those questions to your Google and Microsoft Advertising reps directly, especially about how clicks and conversions from ads in AI Mode and Copilot surface in your reports. Microsoft sat on the working group. Its answers may come faster.

    Sources indicate that the IAB is candid that this is a framework, not a fix. CEO David Cohen mentioned the blueprint “is honest about what the industry can’t yet substantiate.” Much of the evidence needed to support AI claims either isn’t captured or sits inside the AI platforms.

    Recent findings suggest that I’d go further. The PPC managers who wait for ChatGPT, Gemini, and AI Mode to hand over clean, labeled data will spend 2027 defending brand budgets with numbers they can’t explain to a CFO. The ones who start estimating their pathway mix now, with surveys, lift tests, and two-column reporting, will at least be counting the right things.

From powering voice for millions of ChatGPT consumers to enabling drone teleoperation at Skydio and serving as the backbone for roughly 25% of 911 emergency calls in the U.S., LiveKit handles the real-time media layer that production AI applications depend on.

    Recent findings suggest that over 300,000 developers and 5,000+ companies — from leading AI labs to Fortune 500 enterprises — run production workloads on LiveKit. We've raised $181M from investors including Index Ventures, Altimeter Capital, and Salesforce Ventures, and we're growing fast.

    Our product is deeply technical, and we sell into a brand-latest category: voice AI infrastructure. As we grow our Sales team, our AEs, SDRs, and presales engineers need to understand how LiveKit works, and why real-time voice AI is hard, well enough to hold their own in a customer conversation.

    We're hiring a Technical Enablement Engineer to own that. You'll build our technical training program from scratch, so ramp time doesn't depend on pulling engineers off the roadmap. You'll sit on the Sales team, report to our CRO, and have a direct line to the engineers building the product.

    It has been revealed that this is a hands-on, builder-first enablement role. You'll see the impact of your work directly in how fast newly introduced sellers ramp and how confident they are in front of customers.

    are known as the go-to person for tackling tough technical problems.

    can clearly explain complex technical concepts to people who aren't engineers.

    are a fast learner, frequently picking up latest languages and tools.

    Audit what AEs, SDRs, and presales know today and where deals stall on technical gaps.

    Build the core curriculum: LiveKit fundamentals, voice AI architecture, agents, and the competitive landscape.

    Ship hands-on labs and sandboxes so sellers build something real, not just watch slides.

    Run technical onboarding for newly introduced AEs and SDRs, and create a clear technical learning path for presales and Solutions Architects.

    Certify demo and discovery readiness through hands-on exercises.

    Keep technical content current with every product release, working directly with engineering and product.

    Measure what matters: ramp time, time to first qualified technical conversation, assessment pass rates, and seller confidence.

    • It has been revealed that we are looking for a Senior Contracts Manager to take ownership of vendor contracting at Supabase.
    • According to recent reports, this is a hands-on, high-autonomy role with real ownership, for an experienced negotiator who takes pride in making procurement faster while managing risk.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    It has been revealed that we are looking for a Senior Contracts Manager to take ownership of vendor contracting at Supabase. You will be the go-to contracts partner for everything we buy.

    According to recent reports, this is a hands-on, high-autonomy role with real ownership, for an experienced negotiator who takes pride in making procurement faster while managing risk. You will negotiate directly, build the playbooks and workflows that let the business self-serve on low-risk deals, and escalate the right issues to Legal at the right time. We work AI-first in Legal: you will use Claude and Ironclad every day to move faster and with greater accuracy. Your work will shape how procurement and vendor contracting scale as Supabase grows.

    Own vendor contracting end to end.

    Review, draft, and negotiate a high volume of vendor agreements, including MSAs, order forms, SOWs, SaaS and cloud subscription terms, DPAs, and NDAs.

    Serve as the single point of contact for all vendor contracting matters raised by FinOps, IT, Security, and business owners, from intake through signature, renewals, amendments, disputes, and offboarding. As capacity allows, you will also support the broader Commercial Legal team on other matters.

    Apply and further build out our playbook and risk framework independently, and escalate to the Assistant General Counsel, Commercial where a deal falls outside approved positions or raises novel legal risk.

    Negotiate data, privacy, and security terms (DPAs, security exhibits, cross-border transfers) within the Security team’s playbook, and bring in the AGC, Commercial or Privacy for anything outside it.

    Review AI vendor terms, such as training on our data, output ownership, and model changes.

    Build and scale vendor contracting operations.

    Build out and maintain our vendor playbook in Claude, so the whole team works from the same guidance and low-risk deals move without bottlenecks.

    Design and improve intake, triage, and approval workflows with FinOps.

    Sources indicate that own the vendor and procurement workflow in Ironclad, including intake, templates, approvals, and the repository, working with Legal Ops, who own the platform. Use it to track renewals and notice windows with FinOps and flag spend concentration risks.

    Create training and self-serve resources for business partners, and raise the visibility of the contracts function as a business enabler.

    Sources indicate that 6 to 8+ years of experience negotiating procurement, vendor, or technology transactions contracting, ideally buy-side at a U.S. SaaS or technology firm, with deep knowledge of SaaS, cloud, and software licensing terms.

    A track record of negotiating directly with vendors and their counsel, independently and at pace.

    Strong working knowledge of privacy, data protection, and security terms in commercial contracts, including DPA negotiation and international data transfers.

    Experience designing contracting processes that are consistent, transparent, and easy for the business to follow.

    Clear writing and speaking, with the ability to explain legal and commercial risk plainly and the judgment to know when to hold a position, approve a reasonable risk, or escalate.

    Comfort using AI tools, Claude in particular, with sound judgment about when to rely on outputs, how to verify them, and how to protect confidential information.

    A degree in a relevant field (for example, law, economics, or political science), though we value experience over the specific degree.

    Sell-side experience negotiating customer, partner, or reseller agreements for a SaaS or technology organization, which helps you see vendor terms from the other side.

    Hands-on experience with Ironclad or a similar CLM tool (Juro, Docusign CLM) or building AI-assisted legal workflows, ideally with some exposure to AI governance.

    Experience working across jurisdictions or with distributed, international teams.

    Experience at a fast-growing, developer-focused, cloud, security, or open source manufacturer.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Sources indicate that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    In a recent development, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    According to recent reports, once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    In a recent development, we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Industry observers note that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    Senior Deliverability and Compliance Specialist at Kit

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
    • Most Kit creators don't have a dedicated Creator Growth Manager, and when their emails start landing in spam, they need someone who can find the cause quickly and explain it in plain language.
    • You'll also build the playbooks, training, and AI-assisted workflows that help Support and contractors handle more deliverability questions on their own, and you'll partner with our infrastructure engineers as we run more of our sending in-house.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Most Kit creators don't have a dedicated Creator Growth Manager, and when their emails start landing in spam, they need someone who can find the cause quickly and explain it in plain language. We're looking for a Deliverability and Compliance Specialist to own deliverability support for that long tail of creators, run Kit's abuse desk, and make the compliance calls that protect the sending reputation every creator on Kit shares.

    You'll also build the playbooks, training, and AI-assisted workflows that help Support and contractors handle more deliverability questions on their own, and you'll partner with our infrastructure engineers as we run more of our sending in-house. A creator can't build a lasting business if their emails don't arrive, so this work connects directly to our mission.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes digging through headers and bounce logs to find the real cause of a problem, can explain DMARC alignment to a first-time creator without jargon, and is comfortable making a firm call when a situation is gray. You don't wait for someone to tell you what needs fixing. You proactively spot opportunities, identify patterns, and take the initiative to improve deliverability before problems arise.

    You'll report to Alyssa Dulin, Director of Creator Success, and collaborate closely with:.

    Our Deliverability team: a Deliverability Lead who supports our highest-value accounts and leads deliverability education, and a Deliverability Specialist who onboards and ramps up large senders moving to Kit.

    Our infrastructure engineers, who run Kit's sending infrastructure.

    Our compliance and anti-abuse engineers, who build the automated checks that keep spammers off Kit.

    Product Specialists and the Support team, who handle the front line and escalate deliverability issues to you.

    Customer Success Managers (we call them Creator Growth Managers at Kit), Sales and Migrations, and Product Managers.

    First Week: Get set up in Kit, our admin tools, and our support and ticketing systems, and meet our distributed team in Get To Know You chats (GTKYs). Meet the deliverability team and get an introduction on the current projects. Read our deliverability playbooks and SOPs, and get access to the monitoring tools you'll use every day: Google Postmaster Tools, Microsoft SNDS, blocklist monitoring, and our internal delivery dashboards.

    According to recent reports, first Month: Shadow the Deliverability team and Product Specialists on deliverability tickets, account approvals, and abuse reports, then start answering queue tickets with review. Join the daily monitoring rotation (blocklist delisting, Postmaster and delivery monitoring) and the weekly Deliverability team meeting. Learn how account approvals, compliance flags, and our in-house sending platform work. By the end of the month, work deliverability tickets and abuse reports on your own and send your first delisting requests. Project: build a recurring report showing the trending deliverability ticket reasons so we understand what’s causing how to reduce friction for customers and how to solve it.

    First Six Months: Own the deliverability support queue for creators without a dedicated CGM: spam-folder placement, bounces, authentication and DMARC setup, and escalations from Product Specialists. Own compliance end to end, from new-account approvals and compliance flags to pausing or closing accounts that put our shared reputation at risk.Run Kit's abuse desk. You'll write and share a strategy that covers coverage, response-time targets, escalation paths, and quality checks, then put it in place so routine spam, phishing, and blocklist reports follow clear SOPs while you take the hardest cases yourself. Be the go-to contact for day-to-day mailbox provider issues with Microsoft, Gmail, Yahoo, Comcast, and regional providers, and write an incident runbook for blocklistings and provider throttling. Track the queue with a simple scorecard (volume, first response time, and escalation rate) and share what you learn with the team. Run training sessions for Support and ship your first process or AI improvements, like cleaner ticket categorization or better account data for our AI support agent, so more deliverability tickets get solved without escalation..

    Industry observers note that first Year: Deliverability support is faster and more consistent for every creator on Kit, including the ones who never talk to a CGM. Your playbooks, help center articles, and AI-assisted workflows are what Support, CGMs, and contractors reach for first, and fewer tickets need to come to you. You've led at least one cross-team fix with infrastructure for a recurring problem you spotted in the queue, such as an alert when a creator's domain authentication breaks or a check for sudden signup spikes. You're helping shape the internal tooling and alerting our in-house sending needs, and you take part in industry groups like M3AAWG.

    Deep working knowledge of email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, alignment, and BIMI basics), plus the ability to read raw message headers and SMTP bounce and deferral codes.

    Hands-on use of Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS/JMRP, and comfort working with major blocklists (Spamhaus, Abusix, Barracuda, Spamcop, and others) and their delisting processes.

    Data fluency: you can pull bounce, complaint, and engagement data together, find the root cause, and explain it so others can act on it.

    Hands-on abuse handling: you can work an abuse report or escalation start to finish, from finding the account and assessing the evidence to acting, replying to the reporter, and documenting the decision.

    Process building: you can turn repeat work into SOPs, playbooks, and quality checks that a contractor or teammate can follow.

    Clear, calm written communication with creators, teammates, and postmasters.

    Using AI tools to research, summarize, and draft, and helping teammates do the same, with the judgment to keep a person on final compliance calls.

    Experience with MTA logs or delivery observability tools (KumoMTA, PowerMTA, Postfix, Kibana/Elasticsearch, or SQL and BI tools like Mode).

    Familiarity with feedback loops, spam traps, list bombing, and bot-signup patterns.

    Familiarity with CAN-SPAM, CASL, and GDPR as they apply to marketing email.

    Experience with Intercom, HubSpot, or a similar ticketing tool.

    Experience building or tuning AI support workflows or macros.

    4+ years in email deliverability, compliance, trust and safety, or technical support at an ESP, mailbox provider, or high-volume sender.

    Handling escalated customer tickets end to end, including with customers who are frustrated.

    Making account-level compliance or abuse decisions, such as approving, suspending, or closing accounts.

    Working an abuse desk or abuse mailbox directly: spam and phishing complaints, provider and blocklist reports, and escalations.

    Leading the fix for a recurring deliverability or compliance problem that needed help from more than one team.

    Supporting senders on shared IP pools at an ESP.

    Setting abuse or trust and safety strategy, or directing contractors or vendors on a support or abuse queue.

    Working directly with mailbox provider postmaster teams.

    Participating in M3AAWG or other industry groups.

    Creating educational content, like help docs, training, workshops, or podcasts.

    Working with creators, digital entrepreneurs, or small businesses.

    You pick up problems that fall between teams without waiting for permission, and you follow them through until they're closed.

    You test a hypothesis against the evidence before you act, and you frame problems clearly enough that others trust your analysis.

    You protect the reputation every creator shares while staying fair and kind to the creator in front of you, and you help them understand the reasoning behind a decision.

    You turn what you learn into docs, templates, and training that others use, and you adjust how you teach to fit the audience.

    You hold a high bar for your work, and you push back respectfully, with data, when something puts our reputation at risk, even when Sales or leadership would prefer a different answer.

    You share in-progress work and risks early so the team can solve problems together.

    Treating deliverability as a set of macros rather than an investigation that needs judgment.

    Discomfort saying no to a creator or a teammate when our shared reputation is at stake.

    Waiting for someone to assign you work when you can already see the problem.

    Needing a fixed playbook, since our sending stack and processes are changing as we bring more sending in-house.

    Keeping knowledge in your head instead of writing it down for the next person.

    Preferring to work without AI tools.

We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    For this role, we're looking for someone based in North America, with working hours that give us solid US time zone coverage of the deliverability queue.

    Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we're hiring at our level 3 ($118,000 USD). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.
